concepts.title: Final Goods, Intermediate Goods and Double Counting
concepts.definition: A good bought for end use and not re-entering any production process is final, while one bought as an input and used up in making another good is intermediate; adding both while totaling output would count the same value twice.
concepts.key_idea: The use of a good, not its physical nature, decides whether it is final or intermediate; counting inputs twice inflates output.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.1, cotton-yarn-cloth chain and double counting discussion, pages 10-12
question_patterns: how do you decide whether a good is final or intermediate
why must intermediate goods be left out while measuring total output
explain the error of double counting with a production chain example
when does the same commodity act as a final good and when as an input
what happens to the estimate of output if raw materials are counted along with finished products
classify tea leaves bought by a household and by a restaurant as final or intermediate

solution_steps.action: Ask who buys the good and for what use
solution_steps.explain: End use by the ultimate purchaser makes it final; use as an input that is used up makes it intermediate.

solution_steps.action: Check for further transformation
solution_steps.explain: A final good exits the production stream once sold; an intermediate good is about to be changed into another commodity.

solution_steps.action: Count only final values in output totals
solution_steps.explain: Since the value of inputs is already embedded in the price of the finished product, adding both would exaggerate output.

concepts.title: Consumption Goods, Capital Goods and Consumer Durables
concepts.definition: Final goods split into items consumed on purchase, such as food, and durable items such as machines that aid production for years; long-lived household items like cars or televisions share durability with machines yet still serve consumption.
concepts.key_idea: Durability alone does not make a good capital; its role in production does.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.1, paragraphs on capital goods and consumer durables, page 11
question_patterns: separate final goods into consumption goods and capital goods
why are machines treated as capital goods while food is a consumption good
what makes a television a consumer durable though it lasts many years
how do capital goods keep the production process running over time
give examples of goods that are durable yet counted as consumer goods
explain the difference between consumer durables and capital goods

solution_steps.action: Test whether the good is used up at once
solution_steps.explain: Goods extinguished by consumption, like food, are consumption goods.

solution_steps.action: Test whether the good assists production
solution_steps.explain: Tools, machines and buildings that enable production without being transformed are capital goods.

solution_steps.action: Place long-lived household items
solution_steps.explain: Cars, computers and televisions last long and wear out gradually, so they are consumer durables within final consumption goods.

concepts.title: Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment
concepts.definition: Capital wears out as it is used, and the value consumed in a year is depreciation, found by spreading the asset's cost over its expected life; what remains of a year's capital-goods output after replacing worn-out capital is the true addition to the capital stock.
concepts.key_idea: Gross investment includes replacement of worn-out capital; only the balance raises the capital stock.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.1, net investment identity and machine example, pages 12-13
question_patterns: work out the annual depreciation of a machine from its cost and working life
how is net investment obtained from gross investment
find the addition to capital stock after allowing for wear and tear
explain why depreciation is deducted while measuring new capital formation
a machine costing 200 lasts 20 years, what value is used up each year
define depreciation as consumption of fixed capital and compute it

solution_steps.action: Spread the asset cost over its useful life
solution_steps.explain: Straight-line depreciation divides the cost of the capital good by the number of years it is expected to serve.

solution_steps.action: Remove replacement spending from gross investment
solution_steps.explain: Subtracting depreciation from gross investment leaves the net addition to the capital stock.

worked_examples.question: Using Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment, compute the result for cost_of_capital_good = 3, useful_life_years = 3, gross_investment = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Spread the asset cost over its useful life: depreciation_charge = cost_of_capital_good / useful_life_years = 1.0 Step 2: Remove replacement spending from gross investment: net_investment = gross_investment - depreciation_charge = 2.0 Final result: 2.0

worked_examples.question: Using Depreciation, Gross Investment and Net Investment, compute the result for cost_of_capital_good = 4, useful_life_years = 4, gross_investment = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Spread the asset cost over its useful life: depreciation_charge = cost_of_capital_good / useful_life_years = 1.0 Step 2: Remove replacement spending from gross investment: net_investment = gross_investment - depreciation_charge = 3.0 Final result: 3.0

concepts.title: Circular Flow of Income and Equivalence of the Three Methods
concepts.definition: In a two-sector economy firms pay households for factor services and households spend those payments back on the firms' products, so the same aggregate can be read as spending, as output value or as factor income, making the product, expenditure and income methods agree.
concepts.key_idea: One circular flow means GDP measured at any of three points must give the same figure.
question_patterns: explain how income keeps circulating between firms and households
why do the product expenditure and income methods give the same GDP
describe the circular flow in a simple two-sector economy
what happens to aggregate income if households decide to spend more
name the three phases at which national income can be measured
how are factor payments and sales revenue linked in the circular flow

solution_steps.action: Trace the two money arrows
solution_steps.explain: Firms distribute revenue as factor payments; households return those payments as spending on output.

solution_steps.action: Read the flow at three points
solution_steps.explain: Measuring spending received (expenditure method), value of final output (product method) or factor payments made (income method) samples one flow.

solution_steps.action: Conclude the identity
solution_steps.explain: Because it is one circuit, leakage-free spending must equal output value and equal factor income, so all three totals coincide.

concepts.title: Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP
concepts.definition: Each firm's contribution equals the value of its output less the value of inputs bought from other firms, and GDP is the sum of these net contributions across every producing firm in the economy.
concepts.key_idea: Deducting intermediate consumption per firm removes double counting, and summing value added gives GDP.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.2.1, farmer-baker example and Table 2.1, pages 17-18
question_patterns: calculate GDP by the value added method for a chain of firms
find the net contribution of a firm that buys raw material worth 50 and sells output worth 200
how is gross value added of a firm computed from sales and intermediate consumption
sum the value added of a farmer and a baker to obtain total output
use the product method to measure annual output of an economy
a firm sells cloth for 200 using cotton worth 50, what is its value added

solution_steps.action: Deduct intermediate purchases from each firm's output
solution_steps.explain: Value added for the first firm removes its (often zero) input cost; the same is done for the second firm.

solution_steps.action: Repeat for the remaining firm
solution_steps.explain: Each firm's net contribution is its sales value minus inputs bought from other firms.

solution_steps.action: Aggregate the net contributions
solution_steps.explain: GDP by the product method is the sum of value added of all firms.

worked_examples.question: Using Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP, compute the result for output_firm1 = 3, intermediates_firm1 = 3, output_firm2 = 3, intermediates_firm2 = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Deduct intermediate purchases from each firm's output: value_added_firm1 = output_firm1 - intermediates_firm1 = 0.0 Step 2: Repeat for the remaining firm: value_added_firm2 = output_firm2 - intermediates_firm2 = 1.0 Step 3: Aggregate the net contributions: gdp_product_method = value_added_firm1 + value_added_firm2 = 1.0 Final result: 1.0

worked_examples.question: Using Value Added or Product Method of Measuring GDP, compute the result for output_firm1 = 4, intermediates_firm1 = 4, output_firm2 = 4, intermediates_firm2 = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Deduct intermediate purchases from each firm's output: value_added_firm1 = output_firm1 - intermediates_firm1 = 0.0 Step 2: Repeat for the remaining firm: value_added_firm2 = output_firm2 - intermediates_firm2 = 1.0 Step 3: Aggregate the net contributions: gdp_product_method = value_added_firm1 + value_added_firm2 = 1.0 Final result: 1.0

concepts.title: Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change
concepts.definition: Unsold finished goods, work in progress and raw materials held by a firm form its inventory, a stock measured at a point of time, while the difference between a year's production and sales is the change in inventories, a flow that may be intended or a surprise.
concepts.key_idea: Inventory level is a stock; its change is a flow, and only deviations from the intended change are unplanned.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.2.1, inventory and shirt examples, pages 18-20
question_patterns: relate change in inventories to production and sales of a firm
find the closing inventory from opening stock and the change during the year
when is inventory accumulation planned and when is it a surprise
distinguish between stock and flow variables using inventories or a water tank
a firm produces 1000 shirts and sells 600, what happens to its stock
explain why the change in inventories counts as investment

solution_steps.action: Take the gap between production and sales
solution_steps.explain: Output not sold in the year adds to stock; sales beyond current production draw stock down.

solution_steps.action: Update the inventory level
solution_steps.explain: Adding the year's change to the opening stock gives the closing inventory, the stock at year end.

worked_examples.question: Using Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change, compute the result for production_during_year = 3, sales_during_year = 3, opening_inventory = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the gap between production and sales: change_in_inventories = production_during_year - sales_during_year = 0.0 Step 2: Update the inventory level: closing_inventory = opening_inventory + change_in_inventories = 3.0 Final result: 3.0

worked_examples.question: Using Inventories: Stock, Flow and Planned versus Unplanned Change, compute the result for production_during_year = 4, sales_during_year = 4, opening_inventory = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the gap between production and sales: change_in_inventories = production_during_year - sales_during_year = 0.0 Step 2: Update the inventory level: closing_inventory = opening_inventory + change_in_inventories = 4.0 Final result: 4.0

concepts.title: Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side
concepts.definition: GDP can be totaled by adding all final spending on domestically produced goods - household consumption, firms' investment, government purchases and exports - and subtracting the import component embedded in each.
concepts.formula: gdp_expenditure_method = consumption + investment + government_spending + exports - imports
concepts.key_idea: Only final expenditures enter, and imports are deducted because they are not produced domestically.
question_patterns: compute GDP by the expenditure method from consumption investment government and net exports

which components of final expenditure enter the demand-side measure of GDP
given household spending 500 investment 200 government 150 exports 100 and imports 120 find GDP
state the expenditure identity of gross domestic product

solution_steps.action: Add the four domestic final expenditures
solution_steps.explain: Consumption, investment, government spending and export receipts together form total final demand addressed to domestic firms.

solution_steps.action: Remove the imported content
solution_steps.explain: Subtracting imports leaves only the value produced within the domestic territory.

worked_examples.question: Using Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side, compute the result for consumption = 3, investment = 3, government_spending = 3, exports = 2, imports = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the four domestic final expenditures: total_final_demand = consumption + investment + government_spending + exports = 11.0 Step 2: Remove the imported content: gdp_expenditure_method = total_final_demand - imports = 9.0 Final result: 9.0

worked_examples.question: Using Expenditure Method: GDP from the Demand Side, compute the result for consumption = 4, investment = 4, government_spending = 4, exports = 3, imports = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the four domestic final expenditures: total_final_demand = consumption + investment + government_spending + exports = 15.0 Step 2: Remove the imported content: gdp_expenditure_method = total_final_demand - imports = 12.0 Final result: 12.0

concepts.title: Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes
concepts.definition: Since every firm's revenue ends up as payments to the factors it hires, GDP equals the total of wages, profits, interest and rent earned by all households in a year.
concepts.key_idea: The distribution phase of the same circular flow adds up factor incomes to GDP.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.2.3, equation 2.5 and firms A-B example, pages 22-24
question_patterns: measure GDP by summing wages profits interest and rent
find national output from the factor incomes of all households

how does the income method view the same circular flow differently

solution_steps.action: Add the four kinds of factor earnings
solution_steps.explain: Wages for labour, interest for capital, rent for land and gross profits for entrepreneurship exhaust the firms' revenue.

worked_examples.question: Using Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes, compute the result for wages = 3, gross_profits = 3, interest_payments = 3, rents = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the four kinds of factor earnings: gdp_income_method = wages + gross_profits + interest_payments + rents = 11.0 Final result: 11.0

worked_examples.question: Using Income Method: GDP as Sum of Factor Incomes, compute the result for wages = 4, gross_profits = 4, interest_payments = 4, rents = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the four kinds of factor earnings: gdp_income_method = wages + gross_profits + interest_payments + rents = 15.0 Final result: 15.0

concepts.title: Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices
concepts.definition: Factor cost keeps only payments to factors; adding production taxes net of production subsidies gives GVA at basic prices, and adding product taxes net of product subsidies on top raises it to market prices.
concepts.key_idea: Production taxes are fixed per producer while product taxes ride per unit of output; each net pair lifts the valuation one step.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.2.4, CSO 2015 revision discussion, page 25
question_patterns: how do you move from GVA at factor cost to GDP at market prices
distinguish production taxes from product taxes with examples

why does India now report GVA at basic prices instead of GDP at factor cost
where do basic prices lie between factor cost and market prices
given net production taxes and net product taxes, build the full price ladder

solution_steps.action: Raise factor cost by net production taxes
solution_steps.explain: Adding production taxes minus production subsidies converts factor-cost valuation to basic prices.

solution_steps.action: Raise basic prices by net product taxes
solution_steps.explain: Adding product taxes minus product subsidies yields the market-price valuation of GDP.

worked_examples.question: Using Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices, compute the result for gva_factor_cost = 3, net_production_taxes = 3, net_product_taxes = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Raise factor cost by net production taxes: gva_basic_prices = gva_factor_cost + net_production_taxes = 6.0 Step 2: Raise basic prices by net product taxes: gdp_market_prices = gva_basic_prices + net_product_taxes = 9.0 Final result: 9.0

worked_examples.question: Using Factor Cost, Basic Prices and Market Prices, compute the result for gva_factor_cost = 4, net_production_taxes = 4, net_product_taxes = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Raise factor cost by net production taxes: gva_basic_prices = gva_factor_cost + net_production_taxes = 8.0 Step 2: Raise basic prices by net product taxes: gdp_market_prices = gva_basic_prices + net_product_taxes = 12.0 Final result: 12.0

concepts.title: GNP, NNP and National Income Chain
concepts.definition: Adding net factor income from abroad to GDP gives GNP; deducting depreciation gives NNP at market prices; deducting net indirect taxes from that gives NNP at factor cost, which is national income.
concepts.key_idea: Each step removes one wedge: borders (NFIA), capital wear (depreciation) and government price wedges (net indirect taxes).
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.3, GNP NNP NI definitions, pages 25-26
question_patterns: derive national income from GDP using NFIA depreciation and net indirect taxes
calculate GNP when GDP and net factor income from abroad are given
find NNP at factor cost from NNP at market prices and net indirect taxes
how does GNP differ from GDP in treatment of foreign earnings
a country has GDP 1100 NFIA 100 net indirect taxes 150, find national income after depreciation
list the steps connecting gross domestic product with national income

solution_steps.action: Cross the border with net factor income
solution_steps.explain: GNP adds what domestic factors earn abroad and removes what foreign factors earn domestically.

solution_steps.action: Allow for capital wear
solution_steps.explain: Subtracting depreciation converts gross to net national product at market prices.

solution_steps.action: Strip out the tax wedge
solution_steps.explain: First net indirect taxes are indirect taxes minus subsidies; subtracting them from NNP at market prices leaves national income.

solution_steps.action: Arrive at national income
solution_steps.explain: NNP at factor cost is what factors actually receive, and that is national income.

worked_examples.question: Using GNP, NNP and National Income Chain, compute the result for gdp = 3, net_factor_income_from_abroad = 3, depreciation = 3, indirect_taxes = 2, subsidies = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Cross the border with net factor income: gnp = gdp + net_factor_income_from_abroad = 6.0 Step 2: Allow for capital wear: nnp_market_prices = gnp - depreciation = 3.0 Step 3: Strip out the tax wedge: net_indirect_taxes = indirect_taxes - subsidies = 0.0 Step 4: Arrive at national income: national_income = nnp_market_prices - net_indirect_taxes = 3.0 Final result: 3.0

worked_examples.question: Using GNP, NNP and National Income Chain, compute the result for gdp = 4, net_factor_income_from_abroad = 4, depreciation = 4, indirect_taxes = 3, subsidies = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Cross the border with net factor income: gnp = gdp + net_factor_income_from_abroad = 8.0 Step 2: Allow for capital wear: nnp_market_prices = gnp - depreciation = 4.0 Step 3: Strip out the tax wedge: net_indirect_taxes = indirect_taxes - subsidies = 0.0 Step 4: Arrive at national income: national_income = nnp_market_prices - net_indirect_taxes = 4.0 Final result: 4.0

concepts.title: Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income
concepts.definition: Personal income is the slice of national income actually reaching households, found by removing retained earnings, corporate tax and net interest paid by households while adding transfer receipts; disposable income is what remains after personal taxes and fines.
concepts.key_idea: Not all national income lands in household hands, and not all household income is freely spendable.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.3, PI and PDI paragraphs, page 27
question_patterns: derive personal income from national income step by step
why are undistributed profits and corporate tax deducted while finding personal income
compute personal disposable income after personal taxes and fines
what role do transfer payments play in personal income
find the spendable income of households from national income data
how do net interest payments by households adjust the personal income figure

solution_steps.action: Collect the income that bypasses households
solution_steps.explain: Retained earnings, corporate tax and net interest paid by households must come out of national income.

solution_steps.action: Add transfers and deduct the bypassed income
solution_steps.explain: Transfer receipts such as pensions are added because households receive them though nothing is produced.

solution_steps.action: Remove obligatory payments
solution_steps.explain: Personal taxes and non-tax payments like fines leave the disposable part households control.

worked_examples.question: Using Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income, compute the result for undistributed_profits = 3, corporate_tax = 3, net_interest_paid_by_households = 3, national_income = 2, transfer_payments = 2, personal_taxes = 2, non_tax_payments = 1.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Collect the income that bypasses households: household_deductions = undistributed_profits + corporate_tax + net_interest_paid_by_households = 9.0 Step 2: Add transfers and deduct the bypassed income: personal_income = national_income - household_deductions + transfer_payments = -5.0 Step 3: Remove obligatory payments: personal_disposable_income = personal_income - personal_taxes - non_tax_payments = -8.0 Final result: -8.0

worked_examples.question: Using Personal Income and Personal Disposable Income, compute the result for undistributed_profits = 4, corporate_tax = 4, net_interest_paid_by_households = 4, national_income = 3, transfer_payments = 3, personal_taxes = 3, non_tax_payments = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Collect the income that bypasses households: household_deductions = undistributed_profits + corporate_tax + net_interest_paid_by_households = 12.0 Step 2: Add transfers and deduct the bypassed income: personal_income = national_income - household_deductions + transfer_payments = -6.0 Step 3: Remove obligatory payments: personal_disposable_income = personal_income - personal_taxes - non_tax_payments = -11.0 Final result: -11.0

concepts.title: Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator
concepts.definition: Nominal GDP values current output at current prices while real GDP values the same output at base-year prices; their ratio, the GDP deflator, isolates the pure price movement between the two years.
concepts.key_idea: With quantities fixed at current levels, any gap between nominal and real GDP reflects prices alone.
question_patterns: calculate real GDP of the current year at base year prices
find the GDP deflator from nominal and real GDP
why can a doubling of nominal GDP mislead about production growth
a country makes 110 units priced 15 now against base price 10, give real and nominal GDP and the deflator
how does the deflator show the rise in the general price level
compare nominal GDP and real GDP as measures of output

solution_steps.action: Value current output at current prices
solution_steps.explain: Multiplying this year's quantity by this year's price gives nominal GDP.

solution_steps.action: Value the same output at base-year prices
solution_steps.explain: Multiplying this year's quantity by the base-year price strips price changes out, giving real GDP.

solution_steps.action: Ratio the two valuations
solution_steps.explain: Nominal divided by real, scaled by 100, is the GDP deflator showing price movement since the base year.

worked_examples.question: Using Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator, compute the result for current_year_quantity = 3, current_year_price = 3, base_year_price = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Value current output at current prices: nominal_gdp = current_year_quantity * current_year_price = 9.0 Step 2: Value the same output at base-year prices: real_gdp = current_year_quantity * base_year_price = 9.0 Step 3: Ratio the two valuations: gdp_deflator = 100 * nominal_gdp / real_gdp = 100.0 Final result: 100.0

worked_examples.question: Using Nominal GDP, Real GDP and the GDP Deflator, compute the result for current_year_quantity = 4, current_year_price = 4, base_year_price = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Value current output at current prices: nominal_gdp = current_year_quantity * current_year_price = 16.0 Step 2: Value the same output at base-year prices: real_gdp = current_year_quantity * base_year_price = 16.0 Step 3: Ratio the two valuations: gdp_deflator = 100 * nominal_gdp / real_gdp = 100.0 Final result: 100.0

concepts.title: Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index
concepts.definition: The CPI prices a fixed basket bought by a typical consumer in the base year and again in the current year, then expresses the current cost as a percentage of the base cost; the WPI does the same for bulk-traded wholesale goods.
concepts.key_idea: A fixed basket turns price change into a single index number.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec102.txt, section 2.4, rice-and-cloth basket example, pages 30-32
question_patterns: compute the consumer price index from basket costs of two years

solution_steps.action: Cost the basket at base-year prices
solution_steps.explain: Multiply each basket quantity by its base-year price and add across goods.

solution_steps.action: Cost the same basket at current prices
solution_steps.explain: The identical quantities at current prices show what the consumer now pays.

solution_steps.action: Express the current cost as a percentage of base cost
solution_steps.explain: Scaling the ratio by 100 gives the CPI for the current year against the base year.

worked_examples.question: Using Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index, compute the result for quantity_good1 = 3, base_price_good1 = 3, quantity_good2 = 3, base_price_good2 = 2, current_price_good1 = 2, current_price_good2 = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Cost the basket at base-year prices: base_basket_cost = quantity_good1 * base_price_good1 + quantity_good2 * base_price_good2 = 15.0 Step 2: Cost the same basket at current prices: current_basket_cost = quantity_good1 * current_price_good1 + quantity_good2 * current_price_good2 = 12.0 Step 3: Express the current cost as a percentage of base cost: consumer_price_index = 100 * current_basket_cost / base_basket_cost = 80.0 Final result: 80.0

worked_examples.question: Using Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index, compute the result for quantity_good1 = 4, base_price_good1 = 4, quantity_good2 = 4, base_price_good2 = 3, current_price_good1 = 3, current_price_good2 = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Cost the basket at base-year prices: base_basket_cost = quantity_good1 * base_price_good1 + quantity_good2 * base_price_good2 = 28.0 Step 2: Cost the same basket at current prices: current_basket_cost = quantity_good1 * current_price_good1 + quantity_good2 * current_price_good2 = 24.0 Step 3: Express the current cost as a percentage of base cost: consumer_price_index = 100 * current_basket_cost / base_basket_cost = 85.714286 Final result: 85.714286

concepts.title: Limits of GDP as a Welfare Index
concepts.definition: Rising GDP need not mean rising wellbeing because its distribution may be skewed, unpaid non-monetary work and barter escape the accounts, and external harms or benefits carry no market price to correct the measure.
concepts.formula: welfare_gap = gdp_level - true_wellbeing (distribution, non-monetary exchanges, externalities)
concepts.key_idea: Three gaps - uneven distribution, unpriced activity and externalities - keep GDP from tracking welfare closely.
question_patterns: explain why GDP growth may not raise the welfare of most people
how does unequal distribution of income weaken GDP as a welfare measure
why are barter exchanges and home services missed by GDP
what is an externality and how does pollution distort the welfare reading of GDP
list the limitations of using GDP as an index of wellbeing
give an example where GDP rises while most people become worse off

solution_steps.action: Check who receives the output growth
solution_steps.explain: If gains concentrate among a few while the majority's income falls, average output rises but welfare does not.

solution_steps.action: Look for unpriced activity
solution_steps.explain: Household services and barter deals create real value yet never enter monetary accounts, so GDP understates activity.

solution_steps.action: Weigh external effects
solution_steps.explain: Unpaid harms like pollution inflate measured welfare, while unpaid benefits deflate it, since externalities carry no market price.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Farmers sell wheat worth 100 with no inputs, bakers buy wheat worth 50 and sell bread worth 200. Use the value added method to find GDP.

solution_template.explain: 100 minus 0 leaves the full 100 as their contribution.
200 minus the 50 of wheat bought leaves 150.
100 plus 150 gives GDP of 250, avoiding double counting of the wheat.

solution_template.explain: Adding net indirect taxes to national income gives NNP at market prices of 1000.
